entities.name: Augustan History
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Augustan History, produced in the late Roman Empire, is a vital Latin collection of biographies detailing the lives of Roman emperors, their colleagues, and rivals between 117 AD and 284 AD. This work is crucial for understanding the political dynamics, power struggles, and cultural narratives of the Roman Empire during a period of significant crisis and transformation. Composed by a group of anonymous authors known as the Scriptores Historiae Augustae, this compilation includes notable figures such as Hadrian, Septimius Severus, and Gallienus, providing insights into the complexities of imperial rule and succession.

The biographies contained within the Augustan History cover a range of events, from military campaigns to political intrigues. It includes accounts of emperors' successes and failures, often blending historical fact with fiction, which has led to debates about its reliability. The text serves as a vital source for historians studying the early Roman Empire, as it reflects the attitudes and values of the time, particularly regarding legitimacy and authority. The period it covers was marked by the transition from the Pax Romana to the Crisis of the Third Century, a time when the empire faced external invasions and internal strife.

The legacy of the Augustan History is multifaceted; it has influenced countless historical interpretations and literary works over the centuries, shaping the Western understanding of Roman history. Its blend of fact and fiction invites scrutiny and analysis, making it a focal point for discussions on historiography and the nature of historical truth. Furthermore, the text has had a lasting impact on the portrayal of Roman emperors in subsequent literature and art, echoing through the ages as both a historical document and a narrative construct.
